Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The goal of this paper is to construct invariant dynamical objects for a (not necessarily invertible) smooth self map of a compact manifold. We prove a result that takes advantage of differences in rates of expansion in the terms of a sheaf cohomological long exact sequence to create unique lifts of finite dimensional invariant subspaces of one term of the sequence to invariant subspaces of the preceding term. This allows us to take invariant cohomological classes and under the right circumstances construct unique currents of a given type, including unique measures of a given type, that represent those classes and are invariant under pullback. A dynamically interesting self map may have a plethora of invariant measures, so the uniquess of the constructed currents is important. It means that if local growth is not too big compared to the growth rate of the cohomological class then the expanding cohomological class gives sufficient "marching orders" to the system to prohibit the formation of any other such invariant current of the same type (say from some local dynamical subsystem). Because we use subsheaves of the sheaf of currents we give conditions under which a subsheaf will have the same cohomology as the sheaf containing it. Using a smoothing argument this allows us to show that the sheaf cohomology of the currents under consideration can be canonically identified with the deRham cohomology groups. Our main theorem can be applied in both the smooth and holomorphic setting.

Our central result exploits the fact that expansion rates differ among the terms appearing in a sheaf cohomological long exact sequence. By leveraging these differences, we can lift finite dimensional invariant subspaces belonging to one term of the sequence uniquely into invariant subspaces of the term that precedes it. # Constructing Invariant Dynamical Objects for Self-Maps of Compact Manifolds

## Overview and Objectives

The central aim of this paper is to develop a systematic method for constructing invariant dynamical objects associated with smooth self-maps of compact manifolds. Importantly, the maps under consideration are not required to be invertible, which broadens the applicability of the results to a wide class of dynamical systems where classical invertibility assumptions fail. By working in this more general setting, the theory encompasses many naturally occurring maps that arise in both real and complex dynamics.

## The Main Result: Lifting Invariant Subspaces

At the heart of the paper lies a result that leverages the differences in expansion rates within a dynamical system. The key technical insight is to work within a sheaf cohomological long exact sequence and to exploit the disparity between expansion rates in order to control the behavior of invariant subspaces. Specifically, the authors prove that finite-dimensional invariant subspaces can be lifted uniquely from one term of the long exact sequence to the term immediately preceding it. This unique lifting property is the engine that drives the subsequent constructions, as it provides a canonical way to transfer invariant structures across the exact sequence.

## From Cohomology to Currents and Measures

Building on this lifting mechanism, the method allows for the construction of unique currents and measures of a prescribed type. These objects have two essential features: they represent invariant cohomological classes, and they remain invariant under pullback by the map. In this way, the abstract cohomological data is realized concretely through geometric and measure-theoretic objects that reflect the underlying dynamics. This bridge between cohomology and currents is what makes the construction dynamically meaningful.

## The Significance of Uniqueness

A particularly important aspect of these constructions is the uniqueness of the resulting currents. In general, dynamically interesting maps may admit a large collection of invariant measures, so establishing uniqueness within a given class is a nontrivial and valuable achievement. The paper explains that expanding cohomological classes play a decisive role here: when local growth is sufficiently controlled, these expanding classes obstruct the existence of any other invariant currents of the same type. Consequently, the constructed current is not merely one among many, but is singled out as the distinguished invariant object in its class.

## Identifying the Relevant Cohomology

To make the cohomological framework concrete and usable, the authors employ subsheaves of the sheaf of currents together with a smoothing argument. This approach enables them to identify the relevant sheaf cohomology canonically with the deRham cohomology groups of the manifold. The identification is canonical, meaning it does not depend on arbitrary choices, and it ties the abstract sheaf-theoretic constructions to familiar and computable cohomological invariants. Notably, the results are established in a way that applies to both the smooth and holomorphic settings, ensuring that the theory is relevant to real differential dynamics as well as to complex and holomorphic dynamical systems.

# Invariant Currents and Measures via Sheaf Cohomology and Differential Expansion Rates

## Introduction and Motivation

A central problem in smooth and holomorphic dynamics is the construction of invariant objects—currents, measures, and cohomology classes—that capture the asymptotic behavior of iterated self-maps. Given a smooth self-map $f\colon M \to M$ of a compact manifold, one seeks canonical dynamical invariants whose existence and uniqueness reflect the geometric structure of the underlying system. This paper develops a systematic method for constructing such invariant objects, grounded in the interplay between the analytic behavior of the map and the algebraic structure of sheaf cohomology.

The guiding principle is that *differences in expansion rates* can be harnessed to isolate distinguished invariant subspaces. When a dynamical system stretches certain directions or cohomological quantities faster than others, this disparity provides a mechanism for singling out a unique invariant object, ruling out spurious competitors that might otherwise obstruct uniqueness.

## The Cohomological Framework

Our approach centers on a sheaf cohomological long exact sequence naturally associated to the dynamical setting. Within this exact sequence, the induced action of the pullback (or pushforward) operator by $f$ decomposes the relevant cohomology groups according to their asymptotic growth under iteration. The strategy is to compare two competing rates:

- the **cohomological growth rate**, governing how a prescribed cohomology class expands under the action of $f$; and
- the **local growth rate**, measuring the pointwise or fiberwise expansion contributed by the finer sheaf-theoretic data.

The long exact sequence links finite-dimensional invariant subspaces at one level to invariant currents and measures at another. By exploiting the gap between these two rates, one can uniquely lift a finite-dimensional invariant subspace through the connecting homomorphisms of the sequence. This lifting procedure is the technical heart of the construction: it produces, from a purely algebraic invariant, an analytic object—a closed positive current or an invariant measure—that represents the given cohomological class.

## The Main Result

The principal theorem provides a precise threshold condition guaranteeing uniqueness. Specifically, when the local growth is **sufficiently small relative to the growth rate of the cohomological class**, the expanding class *uniquely determines* the associated invariant current. In this regime:

1. **Existence.** The finite-dimensional invariant subspace lifts canonically to an invariant current representing the prescribed class.

2. **Uniqueness.** No competing invariant currents can arise. The domination of the cohomological expansion over the local growth forces any candidate invariant object to coincide with the constructed one, eliminating the possibility of alternative invariant currents that would fragment the dynamical picture.

The mechanism preventing competing currents is essentially a contraction estimate: any deviation from the distinguished invariant object is governed by the subdominant local rate and is therefore driven to zero under iteration, while the principal object persists at the leading cohomological rate.

## Identification with de Rham Cohomology

A significant consequence of the uniqueness result is the **identification of the relevant sheaf cohomology with de Rham cohomology**. Because the invariant current is uniquely pinned down by its expanding class, the abstract sheaf-cohomological invariant can be represented by a genuine differential-geometric object. This identification holds in both the **smooth** and the **holomorphic** settings:

- In the **smooth category**, the invariant currents correspond to de Rham cohomology classes, and the construction yields invariant measures and currents that are canonically attached to the dynamics.

- In the **holomorphic category**, the same framework applies to holomorphic (or Dolbeault-type) cohomology, producing invariant closed positive currents that represent classes in the appropriate complex cohomology, consistent with the expectations of complex dynamical systems.

## Conclusion

By translating dynamical expansion into a competition of growth rates within a long exact sequence, this work provides a unified and robust method for constructing invariant currents and measures. The key insight—that sufficiently dominant cohomological growth suppresses local fluctuations and enforces uniqueness—yields not only the existence of canonical invariant objects but also a clean cohomological interpretation of them. The resulting identification of sheaf cohomology with de Rham cohomology bridges the algebraic and analytic descriptions of the dynamics, offering a versatile tool applicable across smooth and holomorphic settings alike.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper about constructing invariant currents and measures for smooth self-maps of compact manifolds using sheaf cohomology.
counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

We develop a cohomological framework for constructing invariant currents and measures associated to smooth self-maps of compact manifolds. Given a smooth map $f: M \to M$ of a compact oriented manifold, the pullback and pushforward operations on differential forms and currents induce actions on the de Rham and Čech cohomology groups of $M$. We show that the spectral data of these induced actions—specifically the eigenvalues of maximal modulus—govern the existence and regularity of closed positive invariant currents.

Our main construction proceeds by realizing invariant currents as sections of a sheaf of germs of local potentials, whose obstruction theory is controlled by a hypercohomology group interpolating between de Rham cohomology and the sheaf cohomology of pluripotential-theoretic data. We prove that when the dynamical degree $d_k$ associated to the action on $H^k(M)$ strictly dominates the neighboring degrees $d_{k-1}$ and $d_{k+1}$, there exists a nonzero closed positive current $T$ satisfying $f^* T = d_k \, T$, and this current is unique within its cohomology class. The sheaf-theoretic approach allows us to control the singular support of $T$ via a Leray spectral sequence argument, yielding regularity results that are inaccessible through purely analytic methods.

By intersecting invariant currents of complementary bidegree, we construct an $f$-invariant probability measure $\mu$ of maximal entropy $\log d_k$, and we establish its mixing properties through a cohomological decay estimate for correlations. We further show that $\mu$ does not charge pluripolar sets and satisfies an equidistribution principle: preimages of generic points, suitably weighted, converge weakly to $\mu$. Finally, we illustrate the theory with applications to holomorphic endomorphisms of projective varieties, automorphisms of tori and hyperkähler manifolds, and postcritically finite maps, recovering and extending several classical results within a unified cohomological setting.

# Abstract

We develop a cohomological framework for the study of finite-dimensional invariant subspaces arising from the action of holomorphic endomorphisms on complex manifolds, with particular emphasis on the interplay between positive closed currents and their cohomological representatives. Let $f \colon X \to X$ be a holomorphic self-map of a compact Kähler manifold, and let $f^*$ denote the induced pullback operator on the space of currents of bidimension $(p,p)$. We show that finite-dimensional $f^*$-invariant subspaces of currents admit canonical lifts through the deRham cohomology, resolving the obstruction problem posed by the failure of pullback to commute with cohomological projection in the non-algebraically-stable setting.

Our first main result establishes a uniqueness theorem for invariant currents: within each eigenspace associated to a dominant dynamical eigenvalue, the normalized positive closed invariant current is unique, and its cohomology class generates the corresponding invariant line in $H^{p,p}(X,\mathbb{R})$. The proof combines a fixed-point argument on the cone of positive currents with a delicate regularization procedure that preserves the invariance structure.

We then introduce a natural filtration by **subsheaves of currents**, indexed by the local integrability exponents of the potentials, and prove that the associated graded pieces carry an intrinsic $f^*$-module structure. This filtration refines the classical decomposition and detects the singular loci where the invariant currents fail to have continuous potentials.

Finally, we identify the finite-dimensional invariant subspaces with distinguished subspaces of deRham cohomology, yielding an explicit isomorphism between the dynamical invariants of the current-theoretic action and the topological data of $X$. As applications, we deduce rigidity results for the spectrum of $f^*$, establish equidistribution statements for preimages of generic subvarieties, and derive constraints on the possible dynamical degrees compatible with a given cohomological structure. Our methods unify the analytic theory of invariant currents with the algebraic structure of cohomology, and suggest a broader program for lifting invariant data across the potential-theoretic and topological categories.

# Invariant Currents for Non-Invertible Smooth Maps

The construction of invariant currents lies at the heart of the ergodic and geometric theory of holomorphic and smooth dynamical systems, providing the analytic backbone from which equilibrium measures, entropy, and equidistribution results are subsequently derived. For a smooth map $f \colon X \to X$ on a compact manifold, one seeks positive closed currents $T$ satisfying a functional invariance relation of the form $f^* T = \lambda\, T$, where $\lambda$ encodes the dynamical degree governing the growth of the induced action on the appropriate cohomology. When $f$ fails to be invertible—as is typical for endomorphisms of projective space, post-critically nontrivial rational maps, or more general branched coverings—the pullback operation acquires genuine multiplicity, and the pluripotential-theoretic machinery that regularizes and controls such currents must be adapted to accommodate critical behavior and the loss of a well-defined inverse dynamics. In this setting the question of *uniqueness* of the invariant current is not a mere technical refinement but a structural imperative: uniqueness certifies that the current is intrinsic to the dynamics rather than an artifact of a particular limiting or cohomological normalization, and it is precisely uniqueness that underlies the strongest dynamical consequences, including exponential mixing, the equidistribution of preimages and periodic points, and rigidity phenomena that distinguish the canonical invariant object from spurious invariant states. The present paper is devoted to constructing such currents for a class of possibly non-invertible smooth maps and to establishing their uniqueness within a natural cohomology class, thereby anchoring the associated invariant measure as the canonical carrier of the system's essential dynamics.
